dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: This, this, this is a Tapedeck podcast.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: Hey everybody, it's Haitch and welcome to the latest installment of Escape Hatch, your portal into cinematic pocket universes. This week I'm joined as always by my co-host Jason Goldman.

dialogues.name: C
dialogues.text: So my kids are really working overtime on Star Wars. So in that sense, the movie's been a tremendous success.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: And we're joined by legendary Batman: The Animated Series writer Paul Dini.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: I don't even remember the name of the characters. Here's BB Rollydroid. BB Rollydroid is cute. He squeaks in a different way.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: The summer of Jason continues with Don Bluth's 1982 animated dark fantasy, The Secret of NIMH. If you're enjoying the show, we need your help. Take a minute to leave us a 5-star rating and review wherever you listen to your podcasts, or just tell your friends about us, because it really does help new listeners find the show. We also have a Discord server where you can hang out with us online whenever you want, and a Patreon where you can support us and unlock exclusive perks. Links are in the show notes. And now, without further adoon, The Secret of NIMH. All right, so Paul, we're so excited to have you on the podcast today, and obviously the first question I want to ask is, what was it like working on one of the most important cultural iconic interpretations of a critical character. Obviously, I'm talking about your 11 episodes on He-Man.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Mm, that's right. Well, He-Man was an experience and mostly good. And because it was so brand new at the time, I was expecting to go into He-Man right there. And if you had said something else, I would have still worked it toward He-Man. Great. Because He-Man is big this week. That's right. I'm looking forward to seeing the movie.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: We're going on Sunday.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Uh, you know, He-Man was, was really interesting because it was brand new. Nobody knew anything about it. We were creating a lot of bits of the lore as we went around, as we went forward with Filmation. This was like 1982, 1983. I was right out of school, and, and Mattel was, um, you know, had come in with these, these, uh, these figures, and I thought they were really cool because the Star Wars figures were about yay big and, you know, kind of You know, you could pose them and everything, but the He-Man figures were big and massive. They had heft to them, and you could really— yeah, throw them around and everything. And even though you looked at the design, you go, well, He-Man's body is the same as Skeletor's body, same as Beast Man's body. And then they capitalize on that. They came out with— here's Faker, who's an evil double of He-Man, right? You know, he's just He-Man with different color, uh, plastic injected. And all the girl characters had the same body type, just reworked. It was really kind of a stroke of genius that they came out with that. And so I worked on the writing of a bunch of those early episodes in the Bible with, you know, Kirk Gudell and Lou Scheimer. And Tom Ruegger was one of the first writers working on He-Man. That's where he and I met.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: That really was— so I was 14 in 1984. And so in those years just before that, right, when we've got Transformers, G.I. Joe, ThunderCats, He-Man. Like, to me, that's kind of like untouchable. And I was looking at your IMDb page. Obviously, I watched the Flash Gordon cartoon that you worked on as well. Thundarr, The Barbarian. It's just like—

dialogues.name: C
dialogues.text: Love Thundarr.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: Un-fucking-believable run of shows that were happening at that time. It's kind of amazing.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Well, you know, what's really interesting is like everybody working in animation at that time was really young. They were between like 21 and 25 or something. They were just getting into it, and we all wanted to do cartoons, but we wanted to do cartoons like, like the Disney classics or the Looney Tunes or, or something, or the early Hanna-Barbera cartoons. And the only people working, you know, my friend Tom Minton, who was there at the time, he's— I think he may have storyboarded one of the first things I ever wrote at Filmation. He, um, he pointed out that there were young guys starting their career, and then there were older guys, 75 years old in some cases, at the end of their career, making a little extra union time for, uh, their pensions and, and healthcare. And there was nobody in between, so there was nobody really to work— there was no, there was no generation. Yeah, like 20 years older who could teach you the ropes or anything. And most of the writers were there like marking time, like, yeah, I'm doing this now, but I got a sitcom pilot that's really working, and, uh, right out of here. Uh, the only person I ever saw make that work with Sam Simon, who was working at, um, Filmation right around the same time. In fact, I was offered a job there because he was getting ready to leave because he was going off to write, uh, sitcoms and things like that. But, uh, he was working on The Mighty Mouse Show, and then he went off and did, um, I believe he did Taxi and maybe Cheers. And then, uh, he did, uh, of course, The Simpsons. And, and he was a great guy, you know, so And I got to know him better years later after he'd done The Simpsons and I was working at Warner Brothers. But there was really nobody there, you know, just— this is the big advantage we have now is that people getting into the business, they— some of them have come in, they've been 25 and they've been sent to me at 50. Oh, God, I'm happy to learn from you. I can learn some stuff from you. And then you treat those guys more or less like peers or contemporaries because you're all kind of in the same age range. You've all had sort of the same experience growing up. In some cases, they were teenagers when, you know, Batman or whatever was on. So you're all kind of speaking the same language. Right. But we're getting to that big gap again where there's only like the older people and then the new people coming in. And now animation is sort of in the doldrums. Like nothing much is going on. And I think a lot of that is because the companies keep getting bought and sold and whole departments are getting fired and, you know, they clean house. Yeah, totally. Bring in other people.

dialogues.name: C
dialogues.text: What was your first— how did you get— I mean, because you were so young when you started working on that, what was your— you said you're straight out of school, so like, what was the— what was the in there? Like, what was the, uh, how'd you get your foot in the door?

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Well, it was a real lucky break. I'd been writing and drawing, uh, cartoons for my school newspaper. I went to Emerson College, and it was a big focus on comedy. So there was a group called the Comedy Workshop, and there were a lot of young hope, you know, would-be, want-to-be comedians, some who did very well, like Denis Leary and Mario Cantone and Eddie Brill, and my good friend Eddie Gordetsky, who was less a performer, more of a writer, but he went on to write things like Two and a Half Men, Big Bang Theory, created the show Mom. A bunch of other stuff. He worked on SNL, you know, great guy. I've known him all these, all these years. And so it was really kind of like comedy commandos, and I, and I kind of stunk as a performer, but I love drawing cartoons. So I draw cartoons for the local newspaper, for local Boston papers, any place, and I had a really rough scratchy style. But my godfather, whose name is John Kakavas, was a, um, music composer. My dad was a singer, and he knew John, uh, way back when they were in the Army together. And this is in the early '50s, and my dad was kind of a rising crooner at the end of the, the, the big band era. So he was like a boy singer, and he, uh, he was mentored by Perry Como and Tony Bennett, guys like that.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: Jesus.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: And he cut some records, and then, uh, and he remained good friends with John, who went on to become A, one of the top composers for TV shows. So he composed for Kojak and Columbo, did some movies, and then had a very distinguished career working in London and with the London Symphony Orchestra. And so we were always in close contact. And he said, I was finishing up at Emerson College. And I said, well, what does Paul wanna do? And he goes, well, he loves cartoons and he's looking for some direction. And, uh, it turned out they had another— they had a mutual friend who was a fellow named Norm Prescott, who was a DJ in Boston when my dad was singing. Norm went on to become business partners with Lou Scheimer, and together they formed Filmation. Used to see their credit in this sort of swirl at the beginning, you know, going around. And, uh, so Norm happened to be in Boston my last year, my last month in college. He said, once you meet him, show him some of your cartoons. So I did, and he said, this is not the kind of artwork we use on our show because they actually needed people who could draw. And I did, you know, little scratchy drawings of, you know, rats and, you know, crazy people. And he said, uh, but, uh, your gags are really funny, so here's the shows we're doing this year coming up. Come up with some ideas and, you know, we'll see if we can buy some gags off you. So they were doing things like Heckle and Jekyll and Mighty Mouse and Fat Albert and Flash Gordon, you mentioned. And I submitted ideas for all of them and they said, well, you, you can do action as well as, uh, comedy. Your stuff's really rough, but if you want to come out for, you know, for a year, you know, and, you know, we can't promise you much more than that. But so I, I went out, you know, right before graduation I had this job, and then I went out and just started work. And I was 21 years old.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: And where were you living? Like, where, where was Filmation at that point?

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: They're in Reseda, which is way out in the valley. I don't know if you know the San Fernando Valley, but it's like Yeah, there's name—

dialogues.name: C
dialogues.text: name checked in The Karate Kid. That's why I know Reseda. Yeah, that's where Daniel lives. That's where Daniel lives in, uh, in the— in, in The Karate Kid.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Yeah, yeah. It's, it's, you know, you drive through the valley and there's one strip mall filled with, you know, fast food places and gas stations, and that's one little city, and then there's the other, and that's— so there's North Hollywood and Reseda and Tarzana and everything. It's one of those places. So, but Filmation had an office space, uh, there on Sherman Way, and it was, uh, it was this big funky building, and they, and they were doing all the production there at that time, which was around 1980 or so. They did everything there. They recorded in the building, they animated, they, uh, and Lou Scheimer, God bless him, all through the '80s, he said, I'm, I'm going to keep my work in, um, in, in the States. And, you know, Filmation animation was never, you know quite up to what, of course, what Disney was, or even Hanna-Barbera when they were doing Johnny Quest or shows like that. But it was good, consistent stuff. It was on the air, and it was a great break. So I went in and worked with their story people. I met guys like Tom Mitten, Tom Ruger, a few others who were starting their career at the time. And I just wrote everything that came up, and I got to be fast, and I got to be, you know, uh, proficient. And, and the storyboard people would occasionally stop by and say, hey, uh, the script is funny, and And, uh, and, and then, you know, we weren't really supposed to fraternize because that slowed up production. Everything was, you know, work, work, work, get it out there, get it out there. And, uh, occasionally I would like go to lunch with a storyboard guy and we figure out ways to plus it or, or, or do gags and, uh, do better gags and things like that.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: So it was great. Jason and I very rarely fraternize. We try and keep it, you know, very professional.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Yeah, this is when you see each other is like on the screen. It's always like that. And then, uh, then I, I went back to Boston for a while, and then I came out again. And by that time, everything I'd written that first year had aired, and I began getting calls from Hanna-Barbera and Ruby Spears and Marvel Productions. And word was out that I was available and I could turn the scripts in, and it was pretty good. So that, that led to a full-time career.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: I thought it was interesting. I saw your— you, you worked on Star Wars Ewoks. And yeah, just the idea— I think it's 1986 or something, but yeah, the The idea that like this is the only Star Wars content that's available on a screen right now, right? There's just nothing, there are no other movies, there's no other TV shows, there's like, this is it. And like we were starved for what we could get.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: That was not lost on me at the time because they had, I was approached, I had an opportunity to submit, you know, material for Lucasfilm for Ewoks and droids, which were you know, were going to happen. And I was hired by Mickey Herman, who was a producer, uh, under George Lucas, and she was in charge of these animated shows. And I thought, this is really great, you know, I get to work on, on Star Wars, even, you know, for Saturday morning, you know, think of the things I'm going to learn, and it's going to be a great experience. So I went, um, I, I went up and, uh, with a couple of other writers and met George Lucas, and he liked my work for Ewoks.

dialogues.name: C
dialogues.text: Oh, amazing.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: There were— the other writers were for droids. And I thought, you know, this will, this will be fun. Yeah, it's Saturday morning TV. It's kind of goofy, but it's, uh, it's great. And I— and after a while, I was, you know, working there on Skywalker Ranch, living close by in the Bay Area, which I— where I'd grown up in East Bay anyway. So it was like moving.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: Okay, okay.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: And, uh, and literally, I was working out of my folks' home for a while while I was looking for an apartment. My dad would come in and goes, you're not gonna live here, are you? And it's like, no, Dad, I'm only here for, for about 2 weeks. Okay, can it be 1 week?

dialogues.name: C
dialogues.text: Yeah, it can be 1 week.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: And I would drive all the way from the East Bay over to Marin County every day. And eventually—

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: Working on the ranch, like, that's the absolute dream. Like, it's the most magical place in the world.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Yeah, and it was really magical then because it was just starting up. And so— Oh, yeah. A lot of the buildings were up. The tech building was up. We were in a building called the Stables, which was— there's the main house, and it was sort of to the left, off to the back. And the amazing thing about the ranch was George could have made it look like anything. He could have made it look high-tech, industrial.

dialogues.name: D
dialogues.text: Sure.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: And he purposely made it look like a ranch that had been there for 100 years, and the buildings have been retrofitted to— for this new purpose. Like, even in the tech building, there were, there were, like, um, train tracks going in there because they had a small train in the mythology that went in there and picked up grain and everything. And, and our building used to be horse stables, and then they were retrofitted to, to this other purpose. But it was all built with that great sense of design, like a Walt Disney would build something. Like, oh yeah, this was from the 1880s, and now now it's the, the, the 1980s and it's been retrofitted to look, to look like something else. So it was great having that window into his, uh, his, his sense of design and imagination. And yes, it was. And at that point, Star Wars was— it wasn't dead, but it was certainly dormant, you know. And we'd occasionally ask him, you're gonna do more things with Star Wars? He goes, no, those stories are over. I'm gonna do one more Indiana Jones maybe and then call it a day. And I'm gonna— and he'd always say, and then I'm gonna make these little experimental films. And I, you know, I think the world is still waiting for those. But one night he showed some of his, uh, college experimental films, like where he took a camera and mounted it underneath the front of a race car and drove it around a track. And, you know, amazing stuff that he just did in college. And, uh, and it's like, yeah, more of that please. That's, that's like fun. And then, uh, then he was working with his friends like Francis Coppola on movies like, uh Tucker and a few other things, and Labyrinth, Jim Henson. And so it was a very interesting time to work there because he was getting involved in different things. And meantime, we're in the back and we're the only people doing Star Wars. We're doing the Ewoks and the droids and, and, uh, and kind of making up the mythology that, that went along with that. And, you know, we occasionally run things by him and he'd say, yeah, that's good. Or then he'd say, nah, do something else. And then we come up with something else and He would like that. But it wasn't until years later that I was working on The Clone Wars that— and he had a lot of input into that. I was living down here in LA. But then it was sort of like, oh, I get to do real Star Wars. I get to, you know, use a lightsaber and cut people in half and do really cool violent stuff. And then that was a lot of fun. And he was getting involved in it too. And he really apparently really liked working on the shows at that point. And they— those were all being done up at Skywalker.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Crazy. Yeah, crazy.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: It was a great— it was a great learning experience.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: So, and then obviously you got over to Warner Brothers where you worked on Tiny Toons Adventures and Animaniacs and Freakazoid. But the character you are the most closely associated with and most well known for, uh, you know, I want to get into. And part of this, this all sort of came together perfectly. My son is 8 and has just been playing— like, he doesn't generally ask for video games. Um, he usually is just playing LEGO Star Wars or LEGO Fortnite. Yeah. And he was— he's like, Dad, there's a LEGO Batman game coming. Can we please get it?

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Yeah.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: And I, I got it and we started playing it and I'm like, okay, we got to watch Batman '89 because you're not old enough to watch the Nolan one yet. Or actually, really I, I think he's ready to watch the Nolan one, but I'm like, I don't want to start with Nolan and then go back. Uh, you can't go backwards. And I had 2 years ago shown him Batman '66. So like, I did do it in the proper order. Yeah. But '89 was great. And then now we've started watching the animated series. But so how did you get involved with Batman: The Animated Series? What was it like, the original kind of formation of the team and, and kind of getting up and running there? Like you had something that was instantly a complete sensation. I was 22 when it came out. A huge Batman fan, uh, from Dark Knight and from Year One and from, you know, going back stuff I was reading in the '70s and '80s. So what was it like for you showing up and getting into this?

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Well, uh, what had happened was, uh, Lucasfilm had been winding down around 1988. We weren't going to be picked up for any new shows. And yet they had a games division that was, that was up and running. And then they had Pixar, which was just starting. And, uh, so they had the, the, the very first Pixar crew over there making little shorts. But, you know, Lucasfilm was really the only game in town, and it didn't look like they'd be back for any, you know, new Saturday morning series or anything. So I began putting the, the feelers out, and then I, I got— I, I was freelancing on a couple of projects in LA, and then Tom Ruger, who I'd known at Filmation and then I had worked with, you know, he'd call me up and say, hey, you want to write a Scooby-Doo you know, at, uh, Hanna-Barbera, you know, and stuff. It was always fun working with him. He said, I'm starting a new crew with, uh, to work at Warner Brothers, and you like Warner Brothers, right? I said, yeah, I love it. He goes, well, why don't you come down and let's make a deal for you to— we're doing a show called Tiny Toon Adventures with Steven Spielberg. And, you know, you worked with George Lucas, you want to work with Steven Spielberg? And I said, oh yeah, that would be fun. That's a logical extension. Sure. And, uh, I really loved the energy at Warner Brothers when I came down there because again it was pretty young crew all wanting to make things. Like, I want to make my What's Opera doc, I want to make my great piggy bank robbery, I want to make, you know, I want to, I want to— I don't want to necessarily remake those movies, I want to do something that's going to be just as good. So Tom was putting together, and, and Gene McCurdy, who was in charge of the whole thing, was putting together a really interesting unit of writers and artists to, um, to, to kind of recreate the Looney Tunes, uh, spirit. And they were doing the show Tiny Toons, which was not Bugs and Daffy as kids, but them mentoring a new generation of ducks, rabbits, pigs, and skunks and things. And so that was a lot of fun, and I was working with some really terrific, uh, other writers Tom would brought in a writer named Wayne Katz, and he brought in a really brilliant writer, improv actress named Sherri Stoner. And Sherri and I got paired up quite a lot to write things together, or we would bounce ideas off each other. And the three of us, Tom, Sherri, and I wrote the Looney, the Tiny Toons pilot. And we met with Stephen, and we got along pretty well with him. And, you know, he had incredible amount of input and enthusiasm for the project. And so, you know, we were all there jamming on Tiny Toons and it was really, you know, we weren't sure if the show was gonna make it or not 'cause it was something brand new. We were using a bunch of different studios to do the animation. Some of the animation was hit or miss. We really tried to write the best scripts we could. And when it finally got on the air, I think people appreciated the effort because nothing had been like it in a long time. So a lot of people liked it and a lot of people thought this is really funny. This is, uh, you know, kind of got the Warner spirit. It's got some rough edges, but, you know, let's, let's keep going with this. And the studio was very happy with us, uh, Steven Spielberg was very happy. So it was natural that we would want to keep this going because now we have an animation division going at Warner Brothers. And Tom and Steven and Shari were already planning out the next show, which was going to be Animaniacs. And then they were also interested in developing Batman because that had been, you know, the second Tim Burton movie was coming out. And so they said, well, we need a Batman show, naturally. And so, um, uh, I was interested in writing that, and Bruce Timm and Eric Radomski were— Bruce was a storyboard artist and character designer, and Eric was a background designer. And they teamed up with the look of the show. Eric had the really bold idea of using black paper and painting, you know, bright colors on that to give Gotham its distinctive look.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: And Bruce— Samurai Jack did too.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Yeah, I think, I think so. They may have, they may have experimented.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: I think, I think they did.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Yeah. And Bruce did some phenomenal character designs, and they showed that to Jean McCurdy, and she basically within one day said, yeah, yeah, go ahead. And she knew that I liked Batman, and she said, well, why don't you write on Batman? And And so I came in and worked on the development with them. And it was a long, long process and getting the show up and running. And there were a few false starts as far as script direction. And I kind of— and what's so viable is that I was kind of coming and going. I'd left Warner Brothers for a while. I was working on a few other projects. I was still coming in to do occasionally things with Tiny Toons. And then finally they said, Alan Burnett came over to kind of figure out the script, where they were at the scripts. And he said, "I really want you to write a couple of these." So I did, and then he liked them so much, he said, "Come back full time." And I did. So, you know, I did.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: I was shocked to see that Heart of Ice was episode 4. Like, that is very early in the run. And it is 100%, it has got it figured out in terms of what is happening. And I texted you about, us covering Batman and Robin, which is not a movie that I like. But they pull the punch because, "Oh, of course they rescue the wife and she goes back in the freezer or whatever at the end." That is not the case in Heart of Ice. She is dead and he is dealing with it. And just the amount of pathos that you get out of him and out of all of the way that you portray villain characters is really, really something special, especially in a quote-unquote kids animated show.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Well, thank you. I mean, uh, you know, I gotta, I gotta share a lot of the thanks with Gene, who just encouraged us to always do our best. Alan, who gave me, uh, you know, kind of free rein to do what I wanted. And Bruce Timm, who got behind most of my ideas, you know, and just said, yeah, these are, these are good. I mean, I enjoy directing these, and, and, uh, you know, keep going. And so it was, it was, uh, there was a lot of support, but there was, there was a lot of support. There wasn't a lot of hands-on control. It wasn't like years later I would work on superhero shows, and it's like, okay, we need to set a week aside to work in the room and break the stories with all the other writers. And I'm going, can't I just write these like I used to? And it's like, no, no, we need all the writers on the same page. We need the overarching, the big arc for the season, and we need to do all these things. And it was sort of against the way I work because, you know, I write from a very character based point of view. And with something like Batman, yeah, I can, I can see the need for, okay, what's our season umbrella? Where are we going with it? But yeah, it doesn't have to be as tightly controlled as it's been in some of the rooms I've worked in lately.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: It is, I mean, it is a beautiful thing the way it is so episodic and you can pop, like I've been popping around, you know, some of your best episodes and it's easy to just jump in and see it. It was fun, you know, going to Mad Love, which is the last, you know, at least the way they're organized on HBO Max. Is the last episode there, and it's fun. You know, I love the design of the new animated series, right? Yeah. Like, I love just the black suit and the way the Joker looks. Like, it's just so cool. Nightwing and Robin and everybody in there. It's just really— it's something really, really special.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Yeah. Yeah, I mean, that was— some people said, well, why'd you change the look? And it's like, well, they did that all the time in the classic. Constantly.

dialogues.name: C
dialogues.text: Yeah, yeah.

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: I mean, the Bugs Bunny of 1940 1942 is not the same Bugs Bunny of 1949 or '48, you know. It's like, sure, he did evolve and the looks evolved, and they, they, you know, you can see a Bugs Bunny from like 10 years later, he still looks like the same character, but there are, there are differences in the style and then, and, and the, the animation and the design. So it, it's something that I think works very well, that you don't want to hold it in stasis. And also Bruce was learning new things, he felt, you know, visually about the character. And also he had created the look of Superman and he wanted wanted elements of Batman to dovetail visually with elements of Superman. So that was one of the other reasons for the, for the change.

dialogues.name: B
dialogues.text: Well, and then obviously the thing you're best known for is having created Harley Quinn. So what, what was the original inspiration? Where did that, where did that come from?

dialogues.name: A
dialogues.text: Um, well, Harley Quinn initially, it came from— I, I'd written— I was writing this story called Joker's Favor, which dealt with an idea that I've always wanted to do. It just popped into my head that you know, an ordinary guy sort of been pushed around, is having a bad day, you know, somebody is rude to him, and then he just decides, I'm gonna, I'm gonna let that person know how I feel, and he yells at him. It turns out to be the Joker, and it's like the worst person in the world you could yell at. In this case, you cut him off in, in his car, and he just had enough. And then I just— he tries to get away, and then the Joker just kind of goes like, hmm, changes direction of the car to follow him because he's been recognized as the Joker.
